extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students in real analysis/measure theory
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and structural theorems about differentiation of Lebesgue integrals on the line: differentiability a.e. of monotone functions, Poisson-integral boundary behavior, Lebesgue decomposition of monotone functions and Stieltjes measures, and equivalent notions of absolute continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson integral properties (Problems 18–20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is in L^p([−π,π]) define its Poisson integral u(r,θ)=∫_{−π}^{π} f(φ) P_r(θ−φ) dφ. If c_n are the Fourier coefficients of f then u(r,θ)=∑_{n=−∞}^{∞} c_n r^{|n|} e^{inθ}, u is harmonic in the unit disk, and u(r,·) tends to f in L^p as r↑1 for appropriate p. For p=1 or 2 there are norm inequalities; if f∈L^∞ then u(r,θ)→f(θ) uniformly on sets where f is uniformly continuous; if f∈C^2 the Poisson integral is the unique harmonic function with those boundary values; in L^∞ one has weak-* convergence of u(r,·) to f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the Fourier-series representation, harmonicity, L^p convergence as r→1, special cases p=1,2, and L^∞ statements: uniform convergence on continuity sets, uniqueness for C^2 boundary data, and weak-* convergence relative to L^1. These are presented as problem statements to be proved; the text gives the integral definition and the target properties to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of functions of bounded variation is BV (Problem 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are of bounded variation on [a,b], then their product fg is of bounded variation on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem prompt: prove this fact. It is part of a group of problems (21–25) exploring properties of bounded variation functions and their positive/negative variation decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimality property of V+ and V− decomposition (Problem 22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a function f of bounded variation on [a,b], with positive and negative variations V+(f)(x) and V−(f)(x), prove the decomposition f(x)=f(a)+V+(f)(x)−V−(f)(x) is minimal in the sense that if g1,g2 are any two nonnegative monotone increasing functions with f(x)−V−(f)(x) ≤ g1(x) and V+(f)(x) ≤ g2(x) for all x, then V+(f)(x)≤g2(x) and V−(f)(x)≤g1(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem asks to verify the minimality characterization of the canonical decomposition into positive and negative variations; preserves original notation and inequality structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of V+ and V− at continuity points of f (Problem 23)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is of bounded variation on [a,b] and is continuous at x∈(a,b), then both V+(f) and V−(f) are continuous at x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem prompt; uses definitions of positive/negative variation from earlier section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total variation equals sum of positive and negative variations (Problem 24)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f of bounded variation on [a,b], the total variation V(f)(x):=sup over partitions of Σ |f(x_i)−f(x_{i−1})| satisfies V(f)(x)=V+(f)(x)+V−(f)(x) for all x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem prompt: prove equality relating total variation to its positive and negative parts; supremum taken over partitions of [a,x].

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: non-BV and candidate BV functions (Problem 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f(x)=x sin(1/x) for x≠0, f(0)=0 on [−1,1]; prove f is not of bounded variation. For g(x)=x^2 sin(1/x) (g(0)=0) on [−1,1], prove or disprove that g is of bounded variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem asks to analyze oscillatory examples to test bounded variation; suggests contrasting behavior with different x-power factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gamma function analyticity and meromorphic continuation (Problems 26–27)
rubrics_metrics.description: 26(a) Prove Γ(s) is continuous for Re s>0; (b) Use Morera’s Theorem to prove Γ(s) is analytic for Re s>0. 27. Prove Γ(s) extends meromorphically to C with poles at nonpositive integers and satisfies Γ(s+1)=s Γ(s) away from the poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems direct elementary complex-analysis proofs (continuity, Morera, analytic continuation, functional equation) as further properties of the gamma function introduced in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rising Sun Lemma (Lemma 7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let g:[a,b]→R be continuous and let E={x∈(a,b): there exists ξ∈(a,b) with ξ>x and g(ξ)>g(x)}. Then E is open in (a,b); writing E as disjoint union of open intervals (a_k,b_k) we have g(a_k) ≤ g(b_k) for each k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma named for the 'sunrise' picture; remark notes exception possibly when a_k=a. The lemma is used as the geometric core for differentiability results. Proof uses compactness/continuity arguments and contradiction; a modified version handles functions with one-sided limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability a.e. of monotone functions (Theorem 7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is monotone increasing on an interval then F is differentiable almost everywhere: the set of nondifferentiability has Lebesgue measure 0. Extending F' to be 0 at nondifferentiable points makes F' Lebesgue measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: define four one-sided limsup/liminf quotients (U_r,L_r,U_l,L_l) and show U_r<L_l and U_l<L_r almost everywhere using Rising Sun Lemma and a covering/iteration argument; handles discontinuous F via a modification of the lemma. Remarks recall that monotone functions have at most countably many jumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-by-term differentiation of absolutely convergent series of monotone functions (Theorem 7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {F_n} is an absolutely convergent sequence (series) of monotone increasing functions on [a,b], then F'(x)=Σ_n F'_n(x) almost everywhere (where derivatives exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to nonnegative monotone terms; use Theorem 7.2 to get almost-everywhere finiteness and then monotone/absolute convergence arguments to pass differentiation under the series. The proof constructs auxiliary functions and estimates to show tails of derivative series tend to zero a.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: First part of Lebesgue's Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Corollary 7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is integrable on every bounded subset of R then F(x)=∫_a^x f(t) dt is differentiable almost everywhere and d/dx ∫_a^x f(t) dt = f(x) almost everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Theorem 7.3 and approximation by indicators/simple functions, monotone-class arguments to show the set of integrable Borel functions for which the identity holds contains indicators and hence all integrable functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition into indefinite integral + derivative-zero part (Proposition 7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every monotone increasing function F on R decomposes uniquely as F=G+H where G(x)=∫_0^x f(t) dt for some f integrable on every bounded interval (f=F' a.e.) and H is monotone increasing with H'(x)=0 almost everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence constructed by taking f as a.e. derivative and forming G; uniqueness follows from Corollary 7.4. The result separates absolutely continuous part from 'singular' part with zero derivative a.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saltus (jump) functions and derivative zero a.e. (Proposition 7.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {x_n}⊂[a,b] and {c_n},{d_n} are sequences of positive reals with Σ c_n + Σ d_n finite and x_n increasing, then the function F defined by jumps (saltus) at x_n (values specified in the proposition) is monotone increasing with F'(x)=0 almost everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saltus functions are countable sums of jump functions; each jump contributes derivative nonzero only at a point, so derivative is zero off a countable set. This establishes a class of monotone functions with derivative zero a.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition into continuous monotone + saltus (Proposition 7.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any monotone increasing F on R decomposes uniquely as F = G + S where G is continuous monotone increasing (normalized G(0)=0) and S is a saltus (jump) function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: enumerate discontinuities, collect jump masses into S, subtract to obtain continuous G. Uniqueness from structure of jumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous singular measures and concentration on null sets (Proposition 7.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ is a Stieltjes measure with no point masses and its distribution function F satisfies F'(x)=0 at every point of a Borel set E, then µ(E)=0 (i.e., µ gives zero measure to any Borel set where F' vanishes everywhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the Rising Sun Lemma to cover E by intervals whose total µ-mass can be made arbitrarily small; remark: alternative proof via Wiener covering lemma is possible and does not require continuity of F. This isolates the meaning of derivative-zero almost everywhere for continuous monotone functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lebesgue decomposition for monotone functions (Theorem 7.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every monotone increasing function F on R decomposes uniquely as F = G + H + S where G(x)=∫_0^x f(t) dt with f integrable on bounded intervals, H is distribution function of a continuous singular measure (H'(x)=0 a.e.), and S is a saltus function. The function f is the derivative of F a.e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines Propositions 7.5–7.8 and 7.7 to separate absolutely continuous, continuous singular, and discrete jump parts; uniqueness follows from uniqueness of the component decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lebesgue decomposition for Stieltjes measures (Corollary 7.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Stieltjes measure µ decomposes uniquely as µ = f dx + µ_cs + µ_d where f is integrable on every bounded interval, µ_cs is a continuous singular measure, and µ_d is a countable sum of point masses with finite total weight on bounded intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by applying Theorem 7.9 to the distribution function of µ; gives the measure-theoretic form of the decomposition into absolutely continuous, singular continuous, and discrete parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of absolute continuity for Stieltjes measures (Proposition 7.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Stieltjes measure µa, the following are equivalent: (a) µa = ∫ f dx on every bounded interval for some integrable f; (b) for each bounded [a,b] and ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that µa(E)<ε whenever E⊂[a,b] is Borel with Lebesgue measure m(E)<δ; (c) whenever E is Borel with m(E)=0 then µa(E)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard measure-theoretic equivalences of absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue measure; remark notes such µa contains no point masses. Proof references Corollary 7.10 and elementary measure arguments; (c)⇒(a) is essentially Radon–Nikodym in the abstract, but for Stieltjes measures it follows from decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: μ absolutely continuous iff distribution function absolutely continuous (Proposition 7.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Stieltjes measure µ is absolutely continuous iff its distribution function F is absolutely continuous (i.e., small total length of disjoint intervals implies small total variation of F on those intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: (µ absolutely continuous)⇒(F absolutely continuous) via measure control on unions; converse uses covering of Borel set by small total length intervals to get µ(E) small and thus (c) of Proposition 7.11; ties measure-theoretic and function-theoretic notions of absolute continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second part of Lebesgue's Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Corollary 7.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F be monotone increasing on R and let f be its a.e. derivative. Then F(b)−F(a)=∫_a^b f(t) dt for all a<b if and only if F is absolutely continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Theorem 7.9 to decompose F and Proposition 7.12 to identify when the continuous singular and saltus parts must vanish; gives necessary and sufficient condition (absolute continuity) for recovering F from its a.e. derivative.
